title: Generative AI & LLMs
short: Understand how generative AI and large language models work, choose and use them well, build a simple RAG helper and use them responsibly.
learn: Explain the difference between predictive and generative AI
Describe tokens, embeddings, attention and the transformer in simple terms
Identify the strengths and limits of LLMs and choose a model for a task
Call a chat API safely and keep keys secret
Design a basic retrieval-augmented generation system
Recognise deepfakes, bias and privacy risks and apply responsible-use rules

lessons.title: What Is Generative AI?

notes.p: For many years, computer programs followed rules written by humans. A programmer wrote 'if the email contains this word, mark it as spam'. This works for simple problems but fails when the rules become too many or too subtle, such as recognising a face, understanding a sentence or writing a paragraph. **Artificial intelligence (AI)** is the broad field of making computers perform tasks that normally need human intelligence. **Machine learning (ML)** is the approach where, instead of writing the rules, we show the computer many examples and let it discover the patterns itself.

**Generative AI** is a branch of machine learning that creates new content: text, images, audio, video, code and more. It learns the patterns of existing data and then produces new data with similar patterns. When you ask a chatbot to write an email or ask an image tool to draw a landscape, you are using generative AI.

tbl: Which category or value does this input belong to?
Is this UPI message a fraud or genuine?
What new content fits this pattern?
Write a clear warning message about UPI fraud for college students.

notes.p: A discriminative model draws a decision line between classes. A generative model learns how the data itself is built, so it can create fresh examples. Both are useful. Many real products combine them, for example a bank may use a predictive model to detect fraud and a generative model to write the customer's explanation.

notes.diagram: Animated diagram: split screen. Left side 'Discriminative': a photo enters a funnel and comes out as a label card 'Cat'. Right side 'Generative': a short text card 'a cat on a Mumbai balcony' enters a machine that outputs a newly drawn picture. Arrows show the direction of data: input to label, versus prompt to new content.

notes.h: The main families of generative AI

ul: **Text (language models):** write, summarise, translate, explain and answer questions. These are called large language models, or LLMs.
**Images:** create or edit pictures from a text description.
**Audio and speech:** convert text to natural voices, transcribe speech, create music.
**Video:** produce short clips from text or images.
**Code:** suggest, explain and fix program code.
**Multimodal models:** handle more than one type of data, such as reading an image and answering in text.

notes.p: You do not need dates, but the sequence helps. Early chatbots in the 1960s used simple pattern rules. Statistical language models in the 2000s predicted words from counts. Around 2013 to 2016, neural networks improved translation and image recognition. In 2017 researchers introduced the **transformer** architecture, which handled language far better and could be trained on huge amounts of text in parallel. From then, models grew larger and abilities increased. Public chat assistants in 2022 and later brought generative AI to ordinary users, including millions of students in India.

notes.h: Why generative AI became useful now

ol: **More data:** large amounts of text and images are available in digital form.
**More computing power:** GPUs and special chips can perform huge numbers of calculations in parallel.
**Better methods:** the transformer and improved training techniques.
**Easy access:** chat interfaces and APIs mean anyone can use the models without training one.

ul: Students use AI to explain difficult topics, practise questions and prepare for interviews.
Customer support teams in banks, telecom and e-commerce use assistants to answer routine queries in English and Indian languages.
Developers use AI coding assistants to write boilerplate code and tests.
Small businesses create product descriptions, posters and social media captions.
Government and NGOs explore translation and voice tools to reach people in regional languages.

notes.p: It is important to remove wrong ideas early.

ul: It is **not a database of facts**. It generates likely text and may be wrong.
It does **not understand** the world like a human. It has no experiences, feelings or intentions, even when its language sounds personal.
It is **not always up to date**. A model knows only what was in its training data plus anything you give it or a connected tool provides.
It is **not automatically unbiased**. It learns from human-written data, which contains human bias.

notes.warn: Do not treat a fluent answer as a true answer. For health, money, law, exams and security decisions, always verify with trusted sources or a qualified person.

notes.h: Key terms you will keep seeing

tbl: The trained mathematical system that produces outputs
The process of adjusting the model using data
Using a trained model to produce an answer
The internal numbers a model learns; larger models have more
The input you give a model
A large general model that can be adapted to many tasks

notes.p: A model passes through two phases. During **training**, which happens once and costs a large amount of computing power, the model adjusts its parameters to predict data better. During **inference**, which happens every time you ask a question, the fixed model uses what it learned to generate an answer. Your chat does not change the model's learned knowledge. That is why a model does not 'learn from you' permanently in a normal chat.

notes.tip: When you meet a new AI product, ask three questions: What content does it generate? Which model or data powers it? What can go wrong? These keep your thinking clear and careful.

flip: What is generative AI?
AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
How does a generative model differ from a discriminative one?
A generative model creates new data. A discriminative model assigns a label or value to given data.
What is inference?
Using a trained model to produce an output for a new input.
Which 2017 invention improved language models greatly?
The transformer architecture.
Is a language model a database of facts?
No. It generates likely text and can be wrong.

lessons.title: How Large Language Models Work

notes.p: A **neural network** is a mathematical structure made of layers of simple units. Each unit takes numbers in, multiplies them by learned weights, adds them and passes a result on. A single unit is very simple. Millions or billions of them together can capture complex patterns. The weights are the **parameters** of the model. Training is the process of adjusting these weights so that the network gives better outputs.

Think of a student learning to identify mango varieties. At first the guesses are random. After seeing many mangoes and being told the right name, the student's internal sense improves. A neural network improves in a similar way, but with numbers and a clear score for each mistake.

ol: The model receives an input and produces a prediction.
A **loss function** measures how wrong the prediction was and gives a single number.
An algorithm called **backpropagation** works out how each weight contributed to the error.
An optimiser, such as gradient descent, changes the weights a little to reduce the error.
This repeats billions of times over a large dataset.

notes.p: You will study these ideas in detail in the Machine Learning and Deep Learning courses. For now, remember that learning means reducing error by small repeated adjustments.

notes.h: Language modelling: predict the next token

notes.p: An LLM is trained on one main task: given a sequence of tokens, predict the next token. For the text 'The capital of India is', the likely next token is 'New' and then 'Delhi'. To predict well across huge amounts of text, the model must pick up grammar, facts, writing styles, reasoning patterns and even some programming rules. These abilities appear as side effects of getting better at next-token prediction.

code.text:
Input tokens : The  monsoon  arrives  in  Kerala  in
Next token   : June   (probability 0.62)
               early  (0.11)
               the    (0.04)
               ...
The model picks one token, adds it to the input and repeats.

notes.p: Computers work with numbers, so each token is converted into a list of numbers called an **embedding** or vector. Tokens with similar meanings end up with similar vectors. 'Doctor' and 'nurse' are closer than 'doctor' and 'bicycle'. Closeness is often measured with cosine similarity, which compares the direction of two vectors.

code.text:
import math

def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    nb = math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    return dot / (na * nb)

# tiny made-up vectors for illustration
doctor  = [0.9, 0.8, 0.1]
nurse   = [0.85, 0.75, 0.2]
bicycle = [0.1, 0.2, 0.95]
print(cosine(doctor, nurse))    # close to 1, similar
print(cosine(doctor, bicycle))  # much lower, different

notes.p: Most LLMs use the **transformer** architecture. Its key idea is **attention**. When the model processes one token, attention lets it look at all the other tokens in the context and decide which ones matter most. In the sentence 'Riya gave Meera the notes because she was absent', attention helps the model decide whether 'she' refers to Riya or Meera by weighing the other words.

notes.diagram: Animated diagram: a sentence 'Riya gave Meera the notes because she was absent' appears as word boxes. When the word 'she' is highlighted, curved arrows of different thickness go from 'she' to every other word. Thick arrows point to 'Riya' and 'Meera', thin arrows to the rest. Then the layer stack is shown: embeddings -> attention layer -> feed-forward layer, repeated many times, ending in a probability bar chart for the next token.

notes.p: A transformer stacks many layers. Each layer contains an attention step and a feed-forward step that refine the representation of every token. At the end, the model produces probabilities for every possible next token. Because attention compares all pairs of tokens, longer contexts need more computation. This is one reason context windows have limits and long prompts cost more.

notes.h: Stages of building a modern assistant

tbl: Learn next-token prediction on a very large text collection
A base model that continues text but may not follow instructions well
Train on examples of prompts and good answers
Humans or other models rank answers; the model is adjusted toward preferred ones
Answers that are more helpful, safer and better in tone
Add system prompts, filters and monitoring

notes.p: The base model gains broad knowledge. The later stages teach it how to behave as an assistant. This is why two assistants built on similar base models can feel very different.

Larger models with more parameters and more training data often perform better, but cost more to train and run. Smaller models can be fast, cheap and run on a laptop or phone, and with good tuning can be excellent for narrow tasks. Techniques such as **quantisation**, which stores weights with fewer bits, reduce size and memory needs with a small loss of quality.

notes.h: Why models hallucinate, in light of how they work

notes.p: The training goal is to produce likely text, not verified truth. When the model lacks the fact, the most likely continuation may still look like a confident answer. There is no internal alarm that says 'I am guessing'. Training methods and tools such as retrieval from trusted sources can reduce the problem but not remove it.

notes.warn: Do not claim that a model 'thinks' or 'knows' in the human sense. It computes probabilities from learned patterns. This view helps you predict when it will fail.

notes.tip: If you can write a prompt as the beginning of a good document, the model will often continue it well. This one idea explains why examples, roles and formats in a prompt help so much.

flip: What is a parameter?
A learned number, such as a weight, inside the model.

What is an embedding?
A list of numbers representing the meaning of a token or text.
What does attention do?
It lets the model weigh which other tokens in the context matter for the current one.
What does preference tuning do?
It adjusts the model toward answers that people or systems rate as better.

notes.task: Try this yourself: Run the cosine function above. Change the vectors to make 'doctor' and 'bicycle' similar and notice how the score changes. Then explain in two lines why embeddings help a computer compare meaning.

quiz: What is the main pre-training objective of an LLM?

lessons.title: Strengths, Limits and Choosing a Model

notes.p: A carpenter who knows what a saw can and cannot do builds better furniture. In the same way, you will get better results from an LLM when you know where it is strong and where it is weak. This lesson gives a practical map of both, then explains how to choose between models.

ul: **Rewriting and editing:** fix grammar, change tone, shorten or expand text.
**Summarising and extracting:** turn a long passage into key points, or pull names and dates from text.
**Explaining:** describe a concept at different levels, with analogies.
**Translating:** between many languages, including Hindi, Tamil, Bengali and others, although quality varies by language and topic.
**Drafting code:** boilerplate, small functions, tests and comments.
**Brainstorming:** ideas, names, outlines and alternatives.
**Classifying text:** sentiment, topic, intent.
**Facts that need precision:** exact dates, numbers, legal sections, citations and links.
**Long arithmetic and strict logic:** models can slip on multi-step calculations unless they use a calculator or code tool.
**Recent events:** the model knows only what was in training data up to its cutoff date unless search is connected.
**Private information:** it cannot know your marks, your company files or your bank balance unless you provide them.
**Consistency:** answers may differ between runs.
**Knowing what it does not know:** it may answer instead of admitting uncertainty.

notes.diagram: Animated diagram: a radar or bar chart with axes 'Rewriting', 'Summarising', 'Explaining', 'Coding help', 'Exact facts', 'Long maths', 'Recent news'. The bars for the first four grow tall in green, the last three stay short in amber, and small icons (a calculator, a search globe) appear next to the short bars to show tools that can fill the gap.

notes.p: The weak areas can often be improved by connecting the model to tools. A **calculator or code tool** handles exact maths. A **search tool** brings in current information. A **retrieval system** lets the model read your own documents. An **API tool** lets it check an order status or a train booking. Systems that choose and use tools on their own are called agents, covered in a later course.

tbl: Through a company's app or API
Weights can be downloaded and run yourself
Higher, needs hardware or a host
Data can stay on your own machine
Limited to what the provider offers
Can be fine-tuned freely within the licence
Pay for computing, no per-token fee

notes.p: Open-weight does not always mean fully open source. Read the licence. Some allow commercial use and some do not.

notes.h: How to choose a model for a task

ol: **Define the task.** Chat, coding help, extraction, translation, image generation?
**Check quality on your own samples.** Public benchmarks are a guide, but your data matters most. Test five to ten real examples.
**Consider speed.** Smaller models respond faster, which matters for live chat.
**Consider cost.** Estimate tokens per request multiplied by requests per day.
**Consider privacy and rules.** Can this data leave your organisation? Is the tool approved?
**Consider language support.** Test the languages your users actually speak.
**Consider context size.** Will you send long documents?

notes.p: Suppose a college help desk bot receives 2,000 questions a day. Each request uses about 800 input tokens and 200 output tokens. That is 1,600,000 input tokens and 400,000 output tokens daily. If a provider charges a given price per million tokens, you multiply to see the daily cost. Input and output are often priced differently, so check the current price list on the provider's website. The exercise shows why prompts should be short and why smaller models are used for simple tasks.

code.text:
requests_per_day = 2000
input_tokens = 800
output_tokens = 200

price_in_per_million = 0.50   # example number only
price_out_per_million = 1.50  # example number only

cost = (requests_per_day * input_tokens / 1_000_000) * price_in_per_million \
     + (requests_per_day * output_tokens / 1_000_000) * price_out_per_million
print("Estimated daily cost:", round(cost, 2))

notes.p: The prices in the code are made-up numbers for practice. Always use the provider's real, current prices.

Benchmarks are standard tests used to compare models, such as exam-style questions or coding challenges. They are helpful but can mislead. A model may be trained on data that includes the test questions, or a benchmark may not match your task. Treat leaderboard rankings as one input and run your own small test.

ul: Is it correct? Check facts and calculations.
Is it complete? Does it cover every requirement?
Is it consistent? Run the same prompt a few times.
Is it safe? Does it avoid harmful or private content?
Is it useful? Would a real user be satisfied?

notes.warn: Do not rely on a model's description of itself, for example its own size or release date. It may be inaccurate. Use the provider's official documentation.

notes.tip: Start with the simplest approach that could work: a clear prompt on a capable general model. Add retrieval, tools or fine-tuning only when testing shows a real gap.

flip: Name two strengths of LLMs.
Rewriting text and summarising are two. Explaining and drafting code are others.
Name two weaknesses.
Exact facts and recent events are two. Long arithmetic is another.
What is an open-weight model?
A model whose trained weights can be downloaded and run on your own hardware, subject to its licence.
Why test models on your own samples?
Public benchmarks may not match your task or may be contaminated.
How can a model get current information?
By connecting a search or retrieval tool.

notes.task: Try this yourself: Pick a task such as summarising college circulars. Write five sample inputs, run them through two different tools or models, and fill a table scoring each for correctness, speed and clarity. Decide which you would choose and why.

lessons.title: Building with LLMs: APIs, Embeddings and RAG

notes.p: Using a chat app is the first step. The next step is to build your own tool that uses a language model, for example a study helper for your department or a support bot for a small shop. Developers do this through an **API (application programming interface)**, which lets a program send a request to a model and receive the reply. In this lesson you will understand the building blocks. The exact function names differ between providers, so always follow the official documentation of the service you use.

notes.h: Anatomy of a chat API request

notes.p: Most providers accept a list of messages with roles, plus some settings. The structure is similar across services.

ul: **system** message: stable rules for behaviour.
**user** message: the person's input.
**assistant** message: earlier replies, sent back to keep the conversation going.
**temperature** and **max tokens**: control randomness and reply length.

notes.p: The API is stateless. The provider does not remember your earlier requests, so for a multi-turn chat your program must send the earlier messages again each time. This is why long chats cost more tokens.

notes.warn: An API key is like a password that can spend your money. Never write it directly in code that you upload to GitHub, never put it in front-end JavaScript, and never share it in screenshots. Store it in an environment variable and rotate it immediately if it leaks. Leaked keys are found by automated scanners within minutes.

code.text:
import os

# Read the key from the environment instead of writing it in the code
api_key = os.environ.get("AI_API_KEY")
if not api_key:
    raise SystemExit("Set the AI_API_KEY environment variable first.")

notes.diagram: Animated diagram: a Python script on the left puts a 'messages' envelope into an arrow labelled HTTPS and sends it to a cloud box named 'Model API'. A reply envelope returns with generated text. A padlock sits on the arrow to show encryption, and a key icon is stored in a locked box labelled 'environment variable' rather than inside the script.

notes.p: A model cannot know your college rules, your product catalogue or yesterday's circular. Fine-tuning can teach style but is not the best way to add changing facts. The popular solution is **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)**. The idea: before asking the model, find the most relevant pieces of your documents and include them in the prompt, then tell the model to answer only from them.

ol: **Prepare:** split your documents into small chunks, for example a few paragraphs each.
**Embed:** convert each chunk into an embedding vector and store the vectors, often in a vector database.
**Retrieve:** when a question arrives, embed the question and find the chunks with the most similar vectors.
**Augment:** place the best chunks in the prompt as context.
**Generate:** the model writes an answer based on that context, ideally with a note about which chunk it used.

code.text:
Answer the question using only the context in <context> tags.
If the answer is not in the context, reply: 'I could not find this in the documents.'

<context>
[Chunk 1] Hostel gate closes at 9:30 PM on weekdays.
[Chunk 2] Late entry needs written permission from the warden.
</context>

Question: What time does the hostel gate close?

notes.p: RAG reduces hallucination because the answer is grounded in supplied text. It also keeps knowledge current: you update the documents, not the model. It does not guarantee correctness. If retrieval picks the wrong chunk, the answer will be wrong, so test retrieval separately.
The following Python code imitates retrieval using word overlap instead of real embeddings. It shows the idea in a few lines and runs without any library.

code.text:
chunks = [
    "Hostel gate closes at 9:30 PM on weekdays.",
    "Library is open from 8 AM to 8 PM.",
    "Exam fee must be paid before 15 March.",
]

def score(question, chunk):
    q = set(question.lower().split())
    c = set(chunk.lower().split())
    return len(q & c)

question = "When does the hostel gate close"
best = max(chunks, key=lambda c: score(question, c))
print(best)

notes.p: Real systems use embeddings so that 'curfew' can match 'gate closing time' even when no words are shared.

tbl: Limited by context size and your wording
Answers from your own changing documents
Consistent style, format or narrow skill
Needs data and cost; poor for changing facts

ul: Treat any retrieved or user-supplied text as untrusted, because it may contain hidden instructions.
Do not send personal data unless necessary and approved.
Set limits on tokens and requests to avoid unexpected bills.
Log requests safely and review failures.
Show users that content is AI-generated and may contain errors.

notes.tip: Build the smallest version first: one prompt, one function, five test questions. Add RAG or tools only after the simple version works.

flip: What is a system message?

lessons.title: Image and Multimodal AI, and Responsible Use

notes.p: Many modern image generators use **diffusion models**. During training, the system takes real images and gradually adds random noise until only noise remains. The model learns to reverse this process, removing a little noise at each step. To generate an image, it starts from pure random noise and removes noise step by step, guided by your text prompt, until a picture appears.

The text prompt is converted into embeddings, and those guide the denoising so that the picture matches the description. This is why detailed prompts about subject, style, lighting and composition change the result.

notes.diagram: Animated diagram: left to right strip of eight frames. The first frame is pure grey static; each next frame becomes clearer, ending with a clean picture of a cricket ground at sunset. A text prompt box above feeds arrows into every step. A reverse strip below shows the training direction where the clean picture is gradually covered with noise.

notes.p: A **multimodal model** works with several kinds of input or output, for example reading a photo of a handwritten note and explaining it in text, describing a chart, answering a question about a diagram, or turning speech into text and back. It combines the idea of embeddings across types, so that an image and a sentence about it have related representations.

ul: **Study use:** photograph a circuit diagram and ask for an explanation of each part.
**Accessibility:** describe images for visually impaired users and convert text to speech.
**Business use:** extract details from scanned invoices, then summarise them.
**Check always:** model readings of images can miss details or misread numbers, so verify important values.

notes.p: A useful structure is subject, setting, style, lighting and format.

code.text:
A school classroom in a small Indian town during monsoon, children
looking out of the window at heavy rain, warm lamp light inside,
soft illustration style, wide horizontal poster layout, no text.

notes.p: Image tools often draw text badly, so add labels afterwards using a design tool. Specify what to avoid, and generate several versions to choose from.

The same technology that helps creators can also deceive. A **deepfake** is synthetic media, usually a face or voice, that imitates a real person. Voice cloning can copy someone's voice from a short sample. Criminals may use it in scams, for example calling a parent in a cloned voice of their child to ask for urgent UPI money.
**How to protect yourself:**

ul: Pause when a message creates urgency or fear, even if the voice or video seems familiar.
Verify by calling back on the known number, or ask a question only the real person can answer.
Agree a family safe word for emergencies.
Check the source. Look for official posts from the person or organisation.
Look for signs such as odd blinking, mismatched lip movement, strange hands or background, but do not rely only on these, because quality improves quickly.
Report fraud through the national cybercrime helpline 1930 or the cybercrime reporting portal.

notes.warn: Never create or share fake images, voices or videos of real people to harass, embarrass, defraud or mislead them. This can be a criminal offence in India and can cause serious harm. Use only your own content or content you have permission to use.

notes.p: Questions about training on copyrighted material and ownership of AI-generated work are still being decided in courts and by lawmakers in many countries. As a user, take simple precautions: do not claim another artist's style or work as yours, check the terms of the tool for commercial use, and give credit where required. Do not ask an AI to reproduce complete copyrighted books, songs or articles.

Models learn from human data and can repeat stereotypes. An image tool asked for 'a doctor' may mostly show one gender. A hiring tool trained on past decisions may repeat past unfairness. Reduce harm by testing with varied examples, avoiding automated decisions about people without human review, and being open about limitations.

ul: Training and running large models uses significant electricity and water for cooling.
Using a smaller model when it is enough saves cost and energy.
AI changes the nature of many jobs. Skills in judgment, verification, domain knowledge and communication stay valuable.
Access to AI differs between people. Teaching others in simple language is a useful contribution.

tbl: Verify important output before using it
Do not share personal or confidential data
Disclose AI use where rules or trust require it
Test for bias and keep human review for people-related decisions
Do not use AI to harm, deceive or harass
You are responsible for what you publish or submit

notes.tip: A simple test before sharing AI content: 'Would I be comfortable if everyone knew how this was made and could see what it says?' If not, rethink it.

glossary: Generative AI
AI that creates new content from patterns learned in data.
Large language model
A neural network trained on huge text data to predict and generate language.
Token
A small unit of text processed by a model.
Parameter
A learned number inside a model.
Transformer
The neural network architecture based on attention used by most LLMs.
Attention
A method that lets a model weigh the relevance of other tokens.
Embedding
A vector of numbers representing meaning.
Fine-tuning
Further training of a model on specific examples.
RAG
Retrieving relevant documents and giving them to a model to ground its answer.
Hallucination
A confident but incorrect model output.
Diffusion model
A model that creates images by removing noise step by step.
Multimodal model
A model handling several data types.
Deepfake
Synthetic media that imitates a real person.
Open-weight model
A model whose weights can be downloaded and run locally.
interview: What is generative AI?
It is a type of machine learning that creates new content such as text, images, audio and code by learning patterns from existing data.
How does an LLM generate text?
It predicts the next token from the tokens so far, using a transformer network trained on large text collections, and repeats this to build the answer.
What is attention?
It is the mechanism that lets the model weigh how relevant each other token in the context is when processing a token, helping with meaning and references.
Why do LLMs hallucinate?
They are trained to produce plausible text, not verified truth, and have no built-in way to detect when they are guessing.
What is RAG and why is it used?
Retrieval-augmented generation finds relevant documents, adds them to the prompt and asks the model to answer from them. It gives current, private knowledge and reduces hallucination.
When would you choose fine-tuning over RAG?
For consistent style, format or a narrow skill. For frequently changing facts, RAG is usually better.
How would you choose between a hosted and an open-weight model?
I compare quality on my samples, cost, speed, privacy needs, licence and effort. Sensitive data often points to open-weight models run locally.
How do you keep an API key safe?
Store it in an environment variable or secret manager, never in public code or front-end files, set usage limits and rotate it if exposed.
How would you protect yourself from voice-clone scams?
Pause on urgent money requests, call back on a known number, use a family safe word and report fraud to the 1930 helpline.
What are your principles for responsible AI use?
Verify output, protect privacy, be honest about AI use, test for bias, avoid harm and accept responsibility for what I publish.
